description:
We are a multidisciplinary team composed of students specializing in Mechatronics, Data Analytics, and Systems Engineering. We combine our knowledge and skills to develop innovative technological solutions.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we will tackle the challenge of developing health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions, integrating technology, data analytics, and software development to contribute to astronauts' safety and well-being.
summary:
We developed TUMI-HEALT, a health monitoring tool for astronauts on long-duration space missions. On these missions, astronauts are largely responsible for detecting changes in their own health. Radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and closed environments can affect the heart, blood, and sleep, and these changes can go unnoticed.

TUMI-HEALT lets astronauts import cardiovascular, hematological, and sleep measurements. It stores them directly on the astronaut's device and compares them against their personal baseline. Through an interactive body map, the astronaut can view the status of each indicator, understand it with three-tier explanations, and track its evolution over time. The app suggests the next step and allows them to request a medical review. It is an informational tool: it does not diagnose or replace healthcare professionals.
details:
What exactly does it do?

TUMI-HEALT is a support system for astronaut health self-assessment. Specifically, it:

  • Logs and organizes cardiovascular, hematological, and sleep indicators.
  • Compares each measurement against the astronaut's personal baseline, rather than a general average.
  • Displays information on an interactive body map (Body Explorer).
  • Explains each indicator at three levels: simple, why it matters in space, and scientific.
  • Shows trends over time and flags missing data, outdated measurements, and significant variations.
  • Suggests the next step and allows requesting a medical review.

How does it work?

  • Import: The astronaut uploads their measurements from CSV, XML, or XLSX files, with validation for each format.
  • Local Storage: Records are saved in the browser using IndexedDB. Demo profiles are kept separate from personal records.
  • Personal Baseline: The app calculates the astronaut's typical value based on their own samples (for example, their median heart rate).
  • Evaluation: It compares the current value against that baseline and historical data, showing whether it falls within their normal range.
  • Exploration: In Body Explorer, the user selects a region (heart, blood, sleep) to view its latest value and three-tier explanation.
  • Tracking: In My Health Trends, the user sees how their values change over time.
  • Action: The user receives alerts, a suggested next step, and the option to request a medical review.

What are its benefits?

  • Autonomy: Helps the astronaut detect health changes without relying on an on-site physician.
  • Clarity: Does not assume the astronaut knows how to interpret their indicators, as each is explained in plain language.
  • Privacy: Data is stored locally on the device and is never sent to external servers.
  • Transparency: Demo data is clearly labeled as simulated.

What do you hope to achieve? [proposal, adjust to your actual plans]

  • Short-term: Expand real NASA data imports and validate reference ranges against official medical standards.
  • Long-term: Build a self-assessment tool that can be integrated with ground-based flight surgeon support.
